A plague of sheep and oxen ends

A plague struck the sheep and oxen at Rieti. Saint Bonaventure says it ended through the water in which Saint Francis’s hands and feet had been washed.

Status: told by Saint Bonaventure in his Life of Saint Francis (1260s).

Source: Bonaventure, Life of St. Francis (1260s), ch. XIII.6, tr. E. G. S. (Everyman volume, 1925), https://archive.org/details/thelittleflowers00unse

Saint Francis’s touch warms a poor man in winter

On a winter day Saint Francis was riding a poor man’s donkey and had to shelter under a rock for the night. The poor man trembled with cold. Saint Bonaventure says that Saint Francis touched him, and the cold left him.

Status: told by Saint Bonaventure in his Life of Saint Francis (1260s).

Source: Bonaventure, Life of St. Francis (1260s), ch. XIII.7, tr. E. G. S. (Everyman volume, 1925), https://archive.org/details/thelittleflowers00unse

Brother Leo’s temptation leaves after Saint Francis writes, 1224

A brother on La Verna was tempted, and he wanted something written in Saint Francis’s hand. Celano does not name him, but Howell’s note says he was Brother Leo. The brother was afraid to ask, but the Spirit made his wish known to Saint Francis. One day Saint Francis called him. “Bring me paper and ink,” he said, “for I will write down the words of God and his praises, which I have pondered in my heart.” With his own hand he wrote out the Praises of God and a blessing for the brother on one parchment. “Take this paper,” he told him, “and keep it carefully until the day of your death.” The temptation left him at once. The parchment survives at the Sacro Convento in Assisi.

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§49).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §49, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life, as quoted in Paschal Robinson, The Writings of Saint Francis of Assisi, 1906, p. 146, https://archive.org/details/cu31924029364787

Pacifico sees swords and a Tau on Saint Francis

Pacifico was a poet whom the Emperor had crowned, and he was known as the “King of Verses.” He met Saint Francis at a convent of nuns in the March of Ancona. There he saw Saint Francis marked with a cross made by two glittering swords. The next day Pacifico joined the brothers. Later he saw a Tau on Saint Francis’s forehead.

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§106) and by Saint Bonaventure. A Tau is a cross shaped like the letter T.

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §106, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Source: Bonaventure, Life of St. Francis (1260s), ch. IV.9 and XIII.10, tr. E. G. S. (Everyman volume, 1925), https://archive.org/details/thelittleflowers00unse

Elias hears that Saint Francis has two years left

At Foligno Elias saw a vision of an old priest dressed in white. The priest told him that eighteen years had passed since Saint Francis’s conversion. He said that Saint Francis would live two more years, and then the Lord would call him to himself.

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his First Life (§109).

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §109, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

Lady Jacoba arrives with what Saint Francis wanted, 1226

Saint Francis was dying. He asked the brothers to write to the Lady Jacoba dei Settesoli of Rome for ash-colored cloth and almond sweets. Before the letter was sent, someone knocked at the door. It was Lady Jacoba. She brought the cloth and the sweets as if she had read the letter. She also brought wax for candles and incense. The Mirror says the letter named everything except the incense.

Lady Jacoba told the brothers what she had heard in her spirit while she prayed. “Go and visit your father Francis, and hurry, because if you wait you will not find him alive.”

Status: told in the Mirror of Perfection (about 1318) from the memories of the companions.

Source: The Mirror of Perfection, “Of the food and cloth he desired before his death,” 1902 English tr., https://archive.org/details/TheMirrorOfPerfection

Saint Francis speaks to the wolf of Gubbio

The Little Flowers tells that Saint Francis met a wolf at Gubbio. He made the sign of the cross and ordered it, “Come here, brother wolf. I command you in the name of Christ not to harm me or anyone.” The wolf closed its jaws and lay down at his feet.

Status: told in the Little Flowers, compiled after 1322 (earliest dated manuscript 1390).

Source: The Little Flowers of Saint Francis, ch. XXI, tr. T. W. Arnold, https://archive.org/details/littleflowersofs00arno

At Saint Francis’s death, 3 October 1226

A brother sees Saint Francis’s soul as a star

The brothers stood around Saint Francis as he died. Celano says that “his most holy soul was released from the flesh” and that his body “fell asleep in the Lord.” One of the brothers saw the soul of his father go straight up to heaven over many waters. It was like a star as large as the moon and bright as the sun, carried on a little white cloud. Celano says this brother was a man of no small fame, but he chooses not to give his name.

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his First Life (1228–29) and by Saint Bonaventure.

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §110, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

Source: Bonaventure, Legenda maior (1260s), ch. 14, English tr. (Washbourne, 1868), https://archive.org/download/St.BonaventureTheLifeOfSt.FrancisOfAssisi_201903

Larks gather on the roof when Saint Francis dies

Saint Bonaventure says that larks came in great numbers to the roof of the house at the hour of Saint Francis’s death. Larks love the light and fear the dusk, he adds. The Mirror of Perfection says this happened on Saturday evening after evening prayer. It says the larks flew in a circle around the roof and seemed to praise the Lord with their singing.

Status: told by Saint Bonaventure (1260s) and in the Mirror of Perfection (about 1318).

Source: The Mirror of Perfection (compiled about 1318), ch. CXIII, tr. Sebastian Evans, 1899, https://archive.org/details/mirrorofperfecti00leob

Source: Bonaventure, Life of St. Francis (1260s), ch. XIV.6, tr. E. G. S. (Everyman volume, 1925), https://archive.org/details/thelittleflowers00unse

Brother Augustine speaks as Saint Francis dies

Brother Augustine was the minister of the brothers in the Terra di Lavoro. He was dying and had lost his speech long before. At the hour of Saint Francis’s death he cried out in front of the bystanders, “Wait for me, father, wait! See, I am coming with you now!” The brothers asked whom he meant. He answered, “Do you not see our father Francis, who is going to heaven?” Then he died.

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§218) and by Saint Bonaventure.

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §218, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Source: Bonaventure, Life of St. Francis (1260s), ch. XIV.6, tr. E. G. S. (Everyman volume, 1925), https://archive.org/details/thelittleflowers00unse

Assisi’s bishop has a vision of Saint Francis

The bishop of Assisi had gone to the shrine of Monte Sant’Angelo. Celano says he was staying at Benevento on the way back. Saint Francis appeared to the bishop on the night he died and said, “See, father, I am leaving the world and going to Christ.” In the morning the bishop told his companions. He sent for a notary and had him write down the day and the hour. Saint Bonaventure says the bishop was at Monte Gargano.

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§220) and by Saint Bonaventure.

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §220, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Source: Bonaventure, Life of St. Francis (1260s), ch. XIV.6, tr. E. G. S. (Everyman volume, 1925), https://archive.org/details/thelittleflowers00unse

Saint Francis’s body becomes soft and white

Brother Elias wrote within days that Saint Francis’s limbs had been stiff and his body marked by suffering in life. He added that after death Saint Francis’s appearance became very beautiful and shone with whiteness. The stiff limbs became soft “like those of tender children.” Celano and Saint Bonaventure agree that the flesh was white and the limbs were soft. They say the nail marks were black and “formed out of his flesh,” and that the side was red. Celano compares the dark marks to little black stones in a white pavement. Saint Bonaventure compares the side to “a rose most fair.”

Status: told by Brother Elias in his letter of October 1226, by Thomas of Celano in his First Life, and by Saint Bonaventure. The words from Elias’s letter are our translation from the Latin.

Source: Brother Elias, letter to the provinces, 1226, in Wadding, Annales Minorum, vol. 2 (1732), pp. 149–150 (page scan checked), https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_3Dn8hVWLUNwC

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §112–113, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

Source: Bonaventure, Life of St. Francis (1260s), ch. XV, tr. E. G. S. (Everyman volume, 1925), https://archive.org/details/thelittleflowers00unse

A doubting knight tests the nail marks, 1226

Jerome was a knight of Assisi, and he doubted the marks of Saint Francis. After Saint Francis died, Jerome moved the nails with his own fingers in front of his fellow citizens. Then he swore on the Gospels that the marks were real.

Status: told by Saint Bonaventure in his Life of Saint Francis (1260s).

Source: Bonaventure, Legenda maior (1260s), ch. 15, English tr. (Washbourne, 1868), https://archive.org/download/St.BonaventureTheLifeOfSt.FrancisOfAssisi_201903

More accounts from two later books

These accounts come from Celano’s Second Life (1244–47) and the Mirror of Perfection (about 1318). Celano names a witness for some of them. The Mirror keeps the memories of Saint Francis’s companions. Each account below says which book tells it.

The leper disappears in open country, about 1205

Celano’s Second Life says that God had spoken to Saint Francis in prayer and told him to take the bitter in place of the sweet. Soon after, Saint Francis met a leper while riding near Assisi. He got off his horse, kissed the leper, and gave him money. When Saint Francis got back on his horse and looked around, the leper was gone. The country was open, and Saint Francis could not see him anywhere. He was filled with wonder and joy.

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§9). In his Testament Saint Francis says that the Lord himself led him among the lepers.

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §9, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Saint Francis sees through a brother the others admired

The brothers thought highly of one brother. He kept strict silence and confessed his sins only by signs. Saint Francis told them, “Give it up, brothers! Do not praise the devil’s counterfeits in him to me!” He said the brother should be told to confess once a week. The brother put a finger to his mouth and refused. Soon after, he left the Order. The Mirror of Perfection says Saint Francis told the head of the Order that an evil spirit led and deceived this brother.

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§28–29) and in the Mirror of Perfection (about 1318).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §28–29, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Source: The Mirror of Perfection (compiled about 1318), ch. CII, tr. Sebastian Evans, 1899, https://archive.org/details/mirrorofperfecti00leob

Saint Francis foretells the defeat at Damietta, 1219

In the crusader camp before Damietta, Saint Francis told his companion that the Christians would lose if they fought on a certain day. He said that if he told the army he would be thought a fool, and if he kept silent he would not escape his conscience. His companion answered that people had thought him a fool before. The army did not listen to him and lost. Celano says 6,000 men were killed or captured. A note in the English translation gives the date as 29 August 1219.

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (1244–47). Jacques de Vitry wrote from Damietta in 1220 that Saint Francis came to the crusader army there.

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §30, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Source: Jacques de Vitry, letter from Damietta, spring 1220, in Boehmer, Analekten zur Geschichte des Franciscus von Assisi, 1904, pp. 101–102, https://archive.org/details/MN5083ucmf_2

Saint Francis answers Brother Leonard’s silent thought

On the road back from the East, Saint Francis rode a donkey while Brother Leonard of Assisi walked. Leonard thought, “This man’s parents and mine did not play together as equals.” At that moment Saint Francis got off the donkey. He said it was not right for him to ride while Leonard walked, because in the world Leonard had been nobler and more powerful than he. Leonard wept and confessed his thought.

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (1244–47).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §31, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Greccio’s wolves and hail stop after a promise

Wolves were killing animals and people at Greccio, and hail ruined the crops every year. One day Saint Francis was preaching to the people. “To the honor and praise of almighty God, listen to the truth I announce to you,” he said. He pledged his word that the plague would leave them if each of them confessed his sins and did worthy penance. Then the Lord would look on them and multiply them. But if they were ungrateful and went back to their old ways, the plague would return and be worse. Through the saint’s merits and prayers the destruction stopped from that hour. Wolves and hail did no more harm, and when hail came toward their borders it stopped or passed elsewhere. Later the people grew rich and forgot God who had saved them. Celano says the evils returned, with pestilence and the sword, and at last fire destroyed their fortress.

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§35–36).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §35–36, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Saint Francis foretells civil war in Perugia

Saint Francis told the brothers, “The men of Perugia have done much evil to their neighbors.” A few days later he went to Perugia and preached. The knights rode around in arms and disturbed his sermon. He told them, “Hear what the Lord announces to you through me, the little poor man.” He warned that God would make them rise up against one another in civil war. Celano says discord broke out a few days later, and neighbors fought neighbors.

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§37) and in the Mirror of Perfection (about 1318). The Mirror says there was an old hatred between Perugia and Assisi.

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §37, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Source: The Mirror of Perfection (compiled about 1318), ch. CV, tr. Sebastian Evans, 1899, https://archive.org/details/mirrorofperfecti00leob

Saint Francis knows a boy of Lucca is lying

A boy of Lucca came to Assisi and asked with tears to join the brothers. Celano says Saint Francis knew by the Spirit that the boy was not led by the Spirit. Saint Francis said, “Unhappy, worldly boy, why do you think you can lie to the Holy Spirit and to me? Your weeping is worldly, and your heart is not with God.” The boy’s parents arrived to take him home, and he went with them.

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§40). The Mirror of Perfection (about 1318) says Saint Francis was ill in the bishop’s palace at Assisi, and that the boy went down when he heard his relatives’ horses.

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §40, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Source: The Mirror of Perfection (compiled about 1318), ch. CIII, tr. Sebastian Evans, 1899, https://archive.org/details/mirrorofperfecti00leob

A canon named Gideon is healed at Rieti

While Saint Francis lay sick in the bishop’s palace at Rieti, a canon named Gideon asked him for the sign of the cross. Gideon had lived by the desires of the flesh and was in great pain. Saint Francis asked how he could make the sign of the cross over him after such a life. Then he made it and warned him that worse would follow if he returned to his sins. Gideon stood up healed. Celano says many people heard the bones of his loins make a noise like dry sticks breaking. After a short time Gideon went back to his old life, and a roof fell in and killed him.

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§41). A canon is a church official.

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §41, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

The nail clippings end a brother’s temptation

A brother from the Marsica region was tempted. He thought that Saint Francis’s nail clippings would end the temptation. A companion told him that Saint Francis had ordered the clippings thrown away. Then Saint Francis sent for the companion and told him to bring scissors, because he wanted to cut his nails. The companion gave the clippings to the tempted brother, and the temptation left him at once.

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (1244–47).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §42, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Food arrives for the eye doctor’s dinner, Rieti

The doctor who treated Saint Francis’s eyes came every day to the hermitage at Rieti. Saint Francis told the brothers to invite him and give him a very good dinner. The brothers were ashamed, because they had little bread and little wine. Then a woman knocked with a basket of fine bread, fish, crayfish pies, honey, and grapes. The doctor said that neither the brothers nor the people of the world knew Saint Francis’s holiness as they should.

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§44) with the doctor as witness. The Mirror of Perfection (about 1318) says the woman was sent by the lady of a castle about seven miles away, and that this happened at Fonte Colombo.

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §44, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Source: The Mirror of Perfection (compiled about 1318), ch. CX, tr. Sebastian Evans, 1899, https://archive.org/details/mirrorofperfecti00leob

Cloth for six tunics arrives

Saint Francis asked his guardian for cloth for one tunic. A man at the gate offered cloth for six tunics. Saint Francis said, “Thanks be to Him who seems to think of us alone!”

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (1244–47).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §43, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Saint Francis blesses two brothers who have left, Greccio

Two brothers came a long way to Greccio for Saint Francis’s blessing. Saint Francis had gone into his cell for the day, and they left sad. When they had gone a stone’s throw, he called after them. He told them to look back. Then he made the sign of the cross over them and blessed them. Celano says Saint Francis knew their wish through the Spirit. He calls it a miracle.

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§45).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §45, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

A greedy redbreast chick drowns as Saint Francis said

A pair of redbreasts fed at the brothers’ table, and they gave their chicks to the brothers. Saint Francis said, “Look at what our brothers the redbreasts have done.” One chick was greedy and bullied the others. Saint Francis said, “He will come to a bad end yet!” The chick fell into a water vessel and drowned.

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§47) as a warning against greed.

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §47, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Parsley is found in the dark

During Saint Francis’s last illness the cook said he could not find parsley in the dark. Saint Francis told him to bring the first herbs he touched. Among the wild herbs there was a leaf of parsley. Saint Francis said, “Do not say that anything is impossible. Even if I told you to do something beyond your strength, obedience would not lack strength.”

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (1244–47).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §51, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Saint Francis warns of famine and appears after death

Saint Francis told a brother that a servant of God lived on the earth. He said that God would not allow famine to rage against people as long as that servant lived. A few days after Saint Francis died he appeared to the same brother and said that the famine was now coming. Celano says Saint Francis appeared a second time three nights later. Celano himself and others who lived in those years saw the calm and plenty while Saint Francis lived and the famine that followed his death.

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (1244–47).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §52–53, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Saint Francis finds a devil in his pillow, Greccio

Saint Francis’s eyes were bad at Greccio, and he had to use a small pillow against his will. That night he said, “My head trembles and my knees give way, as if I had eaten bread made from weeds. I believe the devil is in this pillow.” The companion who carried the pillow out lost his speech and stood rooted to the spot. He could move again when Saint Francis called him. Saint Francis said he had known at evening prayer that the devil was coming to the cell. He said the devil is crafty, because when he cannot hurt the soul he gives the body a reason to complain.

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§64) and in the Mirror of Perfection (about 1318).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §64, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Source: The Mirror of Perfection (compiled about 1318), ch. XCVIII, tr. Sebastian Evans, 1899, https://archive.org/details/mirrorofperfecti00leob

A brother who takes coins loses his speech

Two brothers found coins near a lepers’ hospital. One of them took the coins and lost his speech. He gnashed his teeth and could say no words. At last he threw the coins away and repented, and his speech came back.

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§66) as a warning against the love of money.

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §66, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Three poor women greet Saint Francis as Lady Poverty

Saint Francis was traveling from Rieti to Siena to have his eyes treated. A physician and some brothers were with him. On a plain near Rocca di Campiglio he met three poor women. They greeted him, “Welcome, Lady Poverty!” Saint Francis gave them coins through the physician. Then the women vanished, and the brothers and the physician saw that the plain was empty. Celano calls it “a wondrous thing, of doubtful interpretation, but most certain truth.”

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§93). The physician and the brothers were with Saint Francis.

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §93, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Bishop Guido cannot speak in Saint Francis’s cell, Portiuncula

While Saint Francis was praying at the Portiuncula, Bishop Guido of Assisi walked into his cell without warning. He began to tremble and could not speak, and he was forced backward. His speech came back when he began to confess his fault.

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (1244–47).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §100, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

An abbot feels warmth when Saint Francis prays

The abbot of San Giustino happened to meet Saint Francis and asked him to pray for him. Saint Francis said he would gladly pray. The abbot walked on a little way. Then Saint Francis said to his companion, “Wait a little, brother. I want to pay a debt that I promised to pay.” Celano says the abbot then felt a warmth and a sweetness he had never felt before. He told many people that it was a miracle.

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (1244–47).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §101, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Demons are driven from Arezzo

Arezzo was torn by civil war. Saint Francis was lodged outside the city, and he saw demons over it. He sent Brother Silvester to the gate to say, “In the name of God, and by order of our father Francis, go far away from here, all you devils!” Silvester went, and before he spoke he praised the Lord and asked his favor. Soon afterward peace came back to the city, and it was governed in quiet. When Saint Francis preached there afterward, he told the people that they had been set free by the prayers of a certain poor man.

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (1244–47).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §108, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

A sow dies after Saint Francis curses it

Saint Francis was lodging at the monastery of San Verecondo in the diocese of Gubbio. A sow there killed a newborn lamb. Saint Francis said, “Alas, brother lamb, innocent creature, you stand for the lasting good of all people! Cursed be the cruel one that killed you, and let no man or beast eat of her!” The sow sickened and died within three days. Celano says it lay in the monastery ditch, dried up like a board.

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§111). This is not the wolf of Gubbio.

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §111, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

A lute plays with no player at Rieti

Saint Francis was at Rieti for the treatment of his eyes. He asked a brother who had played the lute to borrow one in secret to soothe him, but the brother was ashamed of what people would say. That night a lute was heard, and no player could be seen. In the morning Saint Francis said that although he could not hear the lutes of men, he had heard a lute sweeter than theirs.

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (1244–47).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §126, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

A waterfowl, a pheasant, bees, and a cicada

A fisherman gave Saint Francis a waterfowl at the lake of Rieti, and it stayed in his open hands while he prayed. A pheasant sent to him by a nobleman of Siena kept coming back to his cell and would not eat away from him. Bees filled his drinking cup in a cell he had left after a forty-day fast. A cicada on a fig tree near the Portiuncula came when Saint Francis called her and sang with him. She stayed eight days until he let her go.

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (1244–47).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §167–171, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

A hood is pulled from a fire unharmed

A brother came to Saint Francis alone and without permission. Saint Francis ordered the brother’s hood thrown into a large fire. No one dared to take it out, because they feared Saint Francis’s displeasure. Then Saint Francis told them to pull it out, and it was unharmed.

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§154).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §154, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Bones appear on the altar at Monte Casale

Saint Francis told the brothers to move relics from an abandoned church at Monte Casale. The brothers did not do it. Later they found “fine, sweet-smelling bones” on the altar. Saint Francis said, “Blessed be the Lord my God, who has done by himself what you should have done.”

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§202).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §202, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

A purse near Bari turns into a snake

Saint Francis and a companion found a large purse of coins on the road near Bari. Saint Francis said it was a trick of the devil and refused to touch it. The companion kept urging him, so Saint Francis went back with him and a boy as witnesses. He prayed a stone’s throw away and then told the companion to take up the purse. A large snake leapt out of it. Saint Francis said that money is only a devil and a poisonous snake to God’s servants.

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§68).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §68, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

A capon looks like fish at Alessandria

At Alessandria in Lombardy a host served Saint Francis a capon, which is a kind of chicken. A man pretending to be a beggar asked for alms, and Saint Francis sent him a piece of the capon on bread. The man kept it to shame Saint Francis. The next morning he held it up before the crowd, and it looked like a fish to everyone. He then confessed and begged Saint Francis’s pardon, and the meat looked like meat again.

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§78–79).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §78–79, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

A voice in the air defends the Rule

The Mirror of Perfection says that Saint Francis went up a mountain with Brother Leo and Brother Bonizo of Bologna to write the Rule again. The ministers of the Order gathered around Elias and said they would not be bound by that Rule. Saint Francis looked up and said, “Lord, did I not tell you that they would not believe me?” Then everyone heard a voice in the air say, “Francis, nothing in the Rule is yours. Everything in it is Mine. It must be kept to the letter and without any added explanation.” The ministers left confused.

Status: told in the Mirror of Perfection (about 1318) from the memories of the companions. Celano does not tell it.

Source: The Mirror of Perfection (compiled about 1318), ch. I, tr. Sebastian Evans, 1899, https://archive.org/details/mirrorofperfecti00leob

Peace between Assisi’s bishop and governor, 1226

In 1226 Saint Francis was ill, and the bishop of Assisi and the governor of the city had become enemies. The bishop excommunicated the governor, and the governor ordered that no one sell anything to the bishop. Saint Francis added a verse on forgiveness to his Canticle and sent two brothers to sing it in the bishop’s palace. The governor listened with tears and said that he would forgive even the killer of his brother or son. He threw himself at the bishop’s feet, and the bishop lifted him up and embraced him.

Status: told in the Mirror of Perfection (about 1318) from the memories of the companions. The Mirror gives no year. The year 1226 is the time when Saint Francis lay ill in the bishop’s palace. Everyone there held the peace to be a great miracle worked through the merits of Saint Francis. Excommunication cuts a person off from the Church.

Source: The Mirror of Perfection (compiled about 1318), ch. CI, tr. Sebastian Evans, 1899, https://archive.org/details/mirrorofperfecti00leob

A priest’s vineyard yields twenty measures, Rieti

Pope Honorius and his court were at Rieti, and cardinals visited Saint Francis every day at the church of San Fabiano. They came in through the vineyard of the priest there, and its grapes were ruined. Saint Francis asked how much wine the vineyard gave at best, and the priest said thirteen measures. Saint Francis promised to make up the loss if it gave less than twenty measures. At the harvest it gave twenty measures of wine, and no less.

Status: told in the Mirror of Perfection (about 1318) from the memories of the companions.

Source: The Mirror of Perfection (compiled about 1318), ch. CIV, tr. Sebastian Evans, 1899, https://archive.org/details/mirrorofperfecti00leob

Fish arrive in winter for the ill Saint Francis

Saint Francis lay ill in the bishop’s palace at Assisi. He said he did not want to eat, but that he might eat a little of a fish called chub. A man arrived with a tray of three large chub and crayfish. They came from Brother Gerard, the minister at Rieti. The Mirror says that these fish could not be had at Assisi in winter.

Status: told in the Mirror of Perfection (about 1318) from the memories of the companions.

Source: The Mirror of Perfection (compiled about 1318), ch. CXI, tr. Sebastian Evans, 1899, https://archive.org/details/mirrorofperfecti00leob

Bread Saint Francis blessed heals the sick

Saint Francis had bread blessed and broken before he died, and he gave a piece to each brother. Celano says he did this in memory of the Last Supper. The Mirror adds that one brother kept a piece of the bread. After Saint Francis died, many sick people who tasted it were healed at once.

Status: told in the Mirror of Perfection (about 1318) from the memories of the companions. Celano’s Second Life tells of the blessing of the bread, and the Mirror adds the healings.

Source: The Mirror of Perfection (compiled about 1318), ch. LXXXVIII, tr. Sebastian Evans, 1899, https://archive.org/details/mirrorofperfecti00leob

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §217, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Private Visions, Voices, and Struggles

These are things that passed between God and Saint Francis in secret, or that one companion alone saw: a vision, a voice, or a struggle with temptation. The early writers tell them as Saint Francis or the companion told them. Each account says who told it, as far as the book says.

Saint Francis prays for a returning brother at Siena

Celano tells of a well-known brother who left the Order and wandered alone, and who came back after a storm of temptations. When he reached the brothers’ house at Siena, Saint Francis was there. Saint Francis saw him, hurried to a cell, and shut himself in. He told the brothers that he had fled to prayer to free the one who had erred. “I saw in my son something that gave me good reason to be displeased. But by the grace of my Christ, all that led him astray is now gone.” The brother then fell on his knees and confessed his fault.

Status: a private experience Saint Francis told his brothers. Told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§32–33).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §32–33, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Saint Francis sees a devil on a brother’s back

Celano tells of a brother who would not obey Saint Francis’s vicar and followed another brother as his superior. Saint Francis was there, and he sent a messenger to warn him. The brother then threw himself at the vicar’s feet and obeyed. Saint Francis sighed and said to his companion, the messenger: “Brother, I saw a devil on that disobedient brother’s back, gripping him by the neck. When I prayed to the Lord for him, the devil suddenly left in confusion.”

Status: a private sight Saint Francis told his companion. Told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§34).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §34, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

A long temptation leaves Saint Francis at the Portiuncula

Celano writes that for more than two years a very heavy temptation of the spirit weighed on Saint Francis. He afflicted his body, prayed earnestly, and wept many tears. One day he was praying at Saint Mary of the Portiuncula. In his spirit he heard a voice say, “Francis, if you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you can tell a mountain to move, and it will move.” Saint Francis asked which mountain he should move. The answer came, “The mountain is your temptation.” With tears he said, “Lord, let it be as you have said,” and the temptation left him at once.

Status: a private experience of Saint Francis. Told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§115) and in the Mirror of Perfection (about 1318). Celano does not say who told it.

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §115, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Source: The Mirror of Perfection (compiled about 1318), ch. XCIX, tr. Sebastian Evans, 1899, https://archive.org/details/mirrorofperfecti00leob

Saint Francis meets a temptation with seven snowballs

Celano says that a heavy temptation of the flesh came over Saint Francis one night at the brothers’ hermitage at Sartiano. Scourging himself with his cord did not drive it away. He went out into the garden and plunged naked into deep snow. There he made seven balls of snow. He set them before him and said to his body: “See, this large one is your wife. These four are your two sons and two daughters, and the other two are the manservant and maidservant who must wait on them. Make haste and clothe them all, for they are dying of cold! But if the care of them troubles you, serve God alone.” Celano says the temptation left him, and he went back to his cell giving glory to God. A brother who was praying saw it all by the bright moonlight, and Saint Francis was much distressed when he learned of it. He told the brother to tell no one as long as Saint Francis lived.

Status: a private struggle seen by one brother and told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§116–117). Celano gives it as Saint Francis’s answer to a temptation of the flesh.

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §116–117, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Devils beat Saint Francis in a cardinal’s tower

Celano says Cardinal Leo of Santa Croce invited Saint Francis to stay with him in Rome, and Saint Francis chose a secluded tower with nine vaulted rooms. On the first night devils came and beat him long and hard until he was half dead. He called his companion from another room and said, “Brother, stay with me, for I am afraid to be alone. The devils have just beaten me.” He was trembling like a man with a high fever. That night he told his companion why God may have allowed it. Brothers in poor places would suspect him of living in luxury if they heard he was with cardinals. He judged that a man who is an example to others should run from courts. In the morning they told the cardinal everything and said farewell.

Status: a private experience that Saint Francis told his companion. Told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§119–120) and in the Mirror of Perfection (about 1318). The Mirror says Saint Francis called the devils the Lord’s sergeants and went back to Fonte Colombo near Rieti.

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §119–120, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Source: The Mirror of Perfection (compiled about 1318), ch. LXVII, tr. Sebastian Evans, 1899, https://archive.org/details/mirrorofperfecti00leob

Devils attack Saint Francis; a brother sees a throne

Celano says Saint Francis once came with a companion to a church far from any home, sent him to the hospital for the night, and stayed alone to pray. Suddenly he was afraid and his body shook, and he knew that devils were rushing noisily over the roof. Saint Francis went out and made the sign of the cross. To the devils he said, “Do to my body whatever you are allowed to do. I have no greater enemy than my body.” They vanished in shame. At dawn his companion came back and prayed outside the choir, and there he fell into a trance and saw in heaven a seat more glorious than the rest. A voice said it had belonged to one of the fallen angels and was being kept for humble Saint Francis. When the companion asked what Saint Francis thought of himself, Saint Francis answered, “I think I am the greatest of sinners. If God had shown such great mercy to any other wicked man, that man would be ten times more spiritual than I am.”

Status: a private experience. The attack is Saint Francis’s, and the vision is his companion’s. Told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§122–123). Celano does not say who told it, and he does not name the companion. The Mirror of Perfection (about 1318) names Pacifico as the companion and puts the church at Bovara near Trevi.

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §122–123, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Source: The Mirror of Perfection (compiled about 1318), ch. LIX–LX, tr. Sebastian Evans, 1899, https://archive.org/details/mirrorofperfecti00leob

God tells Saint Francis that his Order will last

Celano says that God comforted Saint Francis with visits that assured him his Order would stand. Once he was distressed by the bad example of some brothers. He prayed, and he brought back this answer from the Lord: “Why are you troubled, little man? ... I called the brothers, and I will keep and feed them. When some fall away, I will replace them with others. If a replacement is not yet born, I will cause him to be born. ... Even if the Order were reduced to three, it will always stand firm through my gift.”

Status: a private experience of Saint Francis in prayer. Told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§158) and in the Mirror of Perfection (about 1318). Celano does not say who told it. The Mirror adds that Saint Francis had just prayed, “Lord, I give back to you the family you gave me.”

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §158, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Source: The Mirror of Perfection (compiled about 1318), ch. LXXXI, tr. Sebastian Evans, 1899, https://archive.org/details/mirrorofperfecti00leob

At Siena Saint Francis learns when he serves God

Celano says that Saint Francis hardly let a moment pass without doing some good. One night in a cell at Siena he called his sleeping companions to him. He said, “Brothers, I asked the Lord to show me when I am his servant and when I am not, for I want to be nothing but his servant. He has now answered me: ‘Know that you are my true servant when you think, speak, and do godly things.’ I have called you because I would be ashamed before you if I ever failed in any of these.”

Status: a private experience Saint Francis told his companions. Told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§159).

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §159, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

After death Saint Francis forbids a brother to preach

Celano writes that after Saint Francis died he appeared in a vision to one of his companions, who was busy with preaching at the time. Saint Francis forbade him to preach and told him to walk in the way of simplicity. Celano says that after this vision the brother felt such sweetness that for several days the dew of the father’s words seemed to be dropping into his ears.

Status: a vision of one companion. Told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§195). Celano does not name him.

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §195, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

A vision of crumbs stands for the Rule

Celano says that Saint Francis was very anxious while the brothers discussed the confirmation of the Rule, their written way of life. He saw a vision in the night. He seemed to gather tiny crumbs of bread from the ground for many hungry brothers around him, but he feared they would fall from his hands. A voice from above told him, “Francis, make one host out of all the crumbs, and give it to all who want to eat.” Those who despised it or did not take it with devotion were marked with leprosy. In the morning Saint Francis told his companions about the vision. He was sad that he could not understand it. The voice came again while he prayed: “The crumbs of last night are the words of the Gospel, the host is the Rule, and the leprosy is wickedness.”

Status: a private vision that Saint Francis told his companions. Thomas of Celano tells it in his Second Life (§209). A host is the bread used at Mass. Celano gives no year.

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §209, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

The Lord promises Saint Francis his kingdom in illness

Celano says that one night the pains of his illnesses wore Saint Francis out, and he began to feel pity for himself. He prayed to Christ so that he would not give in. The Lord asked him whether he would not rejoice and gladly bear his sufferings for a treasure of glory greater than all the gold in the world. Saint Francis answered, “I would rejoice indeed, and very much.” The Lord said, “Rejoice, for your sickness is a pledge of my kingdom. Be secure and confident through patience, and wait for the inheritance of that kingdom.” Celano says Saint Francis told his companions a little of his joy, and that it was then that he composed the Praises of the Creatures.

Status: a private experience of Saint Francis. Told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§213). Celano says Saint Francis told his companions a little of it. He gives no place. The Mirror of Perfection (about 1318) puts it at San Damiano. It says his eyes were so sore that for more than sixty days he could not bear daylight, and that mice ran over him night and day.

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §213, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

Source: The Mirror of Perfection (compiled about 1318), ch. C, tr. Sebastian Evans, 1899, https://archive.org/details/mirrorofperfecti00leob

A brother sees Saint Francis in a purple robe

Celano writes that Saint Francis appeared to a brother of praiseworthy life on the night he died, at the very hour of his passing. The brother was praying. Saint Francis wore a purple dalmatic, a long church robe, and a countless crowd followed him. Some in the crowd asked the brother, “Is this not Christ, brother?” and he answered, “It is he.” Others asked, “Is this not Saint Francis?” and he gave the same answer. Celano says it seemed to the brother and to the whole crowd that Christ and Saint Francis were one person.

Status: a vision of one brother. Told by Thomas of Celano in his Second Life (§219). Celano does not name him.

Source: Thomas of Celano, Second Life (1244–47), §219, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/details/livesofsfranciso00thom

An angel announces four promises for the Order

The Mirror of Perfection says that Saint Francis told of four things he had obtained from the Lord for his Order, and that an angel had announced them to him. The Order would not fail until the Day of Judgment. No one who knowingly persecuted it would live long, and no wicked man who meant to live wickedly in it could stay long. Whoever loved the Order from the heart would find mercy at last, however he had sinned.

Status: a private message that Saint Francis told, written down in the Mirror of Perfection (about 1318).

Source: The Mirror of Perfection (compiled about 1318), ch. LXXVIII–LXXIX, tr. Sebastian Evans, 1899, https://archive.org/details/mirrorofperfecti00leob

After Saint Francis’s death: other accounts

Saint Francis’s pillow is honored and his belt cures

Celano wrote in 1228–29 about miracles in France. He says that “the king and queen and all the great men ran to kiss and honor the pillow that Saint Francis had used in his sickness.” He also says that people were cured by pieces of his belt.

Status: told by Thomas of Celano in his First Life (1228–29).

Source: Thomas of Celano, First Life (1228–29), §120, tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell, 1908, https://archive.org/download/the-first-life-of-saint-francis-brother-thomas-of-celano

Pope Gregory IX dreams of Saint Francis’s side wound

Saint Bonaventure says that Pope Gregory IX had doubts about the wound in Saint Francis’s side. Saint Francis appeared to him in a dream with a stern face. He raised his arm, showed the wound, and told the Pope to fill a vessel with its blood. The Pope held the vessel, and it was full to the brim. Saint Bonaventure says Gregory told the story with many tears.

Status: told by Saint Bonaventure in his Life of Saint Francis (1260s).

Source: Bonaventure, Legenda maior (1260s), ch. 15, English tr. (Washbourne, 1868), https://archive.org/download/St.BonaventureTheLifeOfSt.FrancisOfAssisi_201903

A doubting friar dreams of washing Saint Francis’s feet

A friar who preached doubted the marks of Saint Francis. In a dream he saw Saint Francis with muddy feet. He washed the feet and seemed to touch the places of the nails. He woke in tears and confessed his doubt in public.

Status: told by Saint Bonaventure (1260s).

Source: Bonaventure, Legenda maior (1260s), ch. 15, English tr. (Washbourne, 1868), https://archive.org/download/St.BonaventureTheLifeOfSt.FrancisOfAssisi_201903

John of Ilerda is healed of stab wounds

Saint Bonaventure tells of a man named John in Ilerda in Catalonia. Men who mistook him for someone else stabbed him many times. The pus from one wound put out six candles, and no doctor could cure him. John called on Saint Francis and Saint Clare. He said that a man in a friar’s robe came in by the window and unwrapped his bandages. John was healed.

Status: told by Saint Bonaventure in his Life of Saint Francis (1260s).

Source: Bonaventure, Legenda maior (1260s), ch. 15, English tr. (Washbourne, 1868), https://archive.org/download/St.BonaventureTheLifeOfSt.FrancisOfAssisi_201903

Roger of Potenza doubts and is wounded

A canon named Roger of Potenza looked at a picture of Saint Francis and doubted the marks. He received a wound like an arrow’s in his palm. He was healed after he confessed. Saint Bonaventure says the bishop’s seal confirmed the account.

Status: told by Saint Bonaventure (1260s). He says the bishop’s seal confirmed it. A canon is a church official.

Source: Bonaventure, Legenda maior (1260s), ch. 15, English tr. (Washbourne, 1868), https://archive.org/download/St.BonaventureTheLifeOfSt.FrancisOfAssisi_201903

Marks on a portrait of Saint Francis vanish, Rome

A noble Roman lady saw the marks of Saint Francis appear on a painted portrait of him. Her daughter swore that the portrait had not shown them before. Then the lady doubted, and the marks vanished.

Status: told by Saint Bonaventure (1260s).

Source: Bonaventure, Legenda maior (1260s), ch. 15, English tr. (Washbourne, 1868), https://archive.org/download/St.BonaventureTheLifeOfSt.FrancisOfAssisi_201903

Saint Bonaventure says many were raised from the dead

Saint Bonaventure says that many people were raised from the dead through Saint Francis, and he tells several cases. A woman at Monte Marcano near Benevento rose from her bier to confess a sin she had never confessed. Then she died in peace. A girl at Parmaco in Apulia was raised after her mother called on Saint Francis. Saint Bonaventure also tells of cases at Nocera, Rome, Capua, Colonna, and Ragusa. He says Pope Gregory IX wrote of another man raised in Germany, but that he himself does not know the story.

Status: told by Saint Bonaventure in his Life of Saint Francis (1260s).

Source: Bonaventure, Legenda maior (1260s), ch. 15, English tr. (Washbourne, 1868), https://archive.org/download/St.BonaventureTheLifeOfSt.FrancisOfAssisi_201903

Pope Nicholas V sees Saint Francis upright, 1449

The Franciscan history Annales Minorum prints a letter that tells a story from 1449. In the letter a bishop named Jacopo says that Cardinal Astorgio told him what he saw at the tomb with Pope Nicholas V. They went down at night and found Saint Francis’s body standing upright. It faced west, with its eyes raised to heaven and its hands hidden in the robe. The wounds showed fresh blood. The letter says the Pope promised to keep the sight secret.

Status: told in a letter of 1449 by Bishop Jacopo of Lacedonia, who heard it from Cardinal Astorgio. Printed in Wadding’s Annales Minorum, 1732.

Source: Wadding, Annales Minorum, vol. 2 (1732), pp. 236–238, https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_3Dn8hVWLUNwC

teachings.teachings:
Francis wrote little, and simply. His Rules, his Testament, a handful of letters, short sayings called Admonitions, and his songs of praise survive. The passages below are our own English translations: the Latin from the 1904 Quaracchi critical edition, and the Canticle from the thirteenth-century Assisi manuscript. The Testament, the letter to Leo, the Praises, and the last will for Clare were checked against page scans of that edition; the other Latin was read in a scanned text. The famous prayer that begins “Lord, make me an instrument of your peace” is not his; it was first printed, unsigned, in Paris in 1912.

What was bitter became sweet

For Francis, conversion began with the thing he could least bear. The Lord “led” him among the lepers, he wrote, and what had been bitter turned into sweetness. His own account puts that change at the root of his new life.

“When I was in sins, it seemed too bitter to me to see lepers. The Lord himself led me among them, and I showed them mercy. And when I left them, what had seemed bitter to me turned into sweetness of soul and body.”

— Francis of Assisi, Testament, 1226 (our translation from the Latin)

He left these words in his Testament, near the end of his life, and put them first, before anything else he wanted his brothers to remember. He lived them: he kissed a leper’s hand on the road, gave alms in the leper house, and near death still wanted to go back and serve the lepers.

The form of the Gospel

Francis believed God had shown him a way of life that was simply the Gospel, lived literally. His brothers were to own nothing, because Christ had made himself poor.

“The Most High himself showed me that I should live according to the form of the holy Gospel. And I had it written in a few words and simply, and the lord pope confirmed it for me.”

— Francis of Assisi, Testament, 1226 (our translation from the Latin)

In the Rule of 1223 he wrote: “The brothers shall make nothing their own, not house, nor place, nor anything. … For the Lord made himself poor for us in this world.” He asked that his words be understood “simply and purely,” as they were written. When he heard the Gospel of the sending of the Twelve, he threw away his shoes, staff, and belt, and he died in a habit that had been lent to him.

Brothers who mother each other

Francis asked his brothers to care for each other with a mother’s tenderness, and he used the same image for every Christian who carries Christ in the heart.

“For if a mother feeds and loves her son in the flesh, how much more carefully should one love and feed his spiritual brother?”

— Francis of Assisi, Rule of 1223, ch. 6 (our translation from the Latin)

In his Letter to All the Faithful he wrote: “We are his mothers when we carry him in heart and body through love and a pure and sincere conscience.” In a note to Brother Leo, written in his own hand, he spoke “as a mother would,” and ended: “if you need it for your soul, or for some other comfort, and you want, Leo, to come to me, come.”

Mercy without limit

Francis could be severe with brothers who refused the Rule, but he asked those in charge to be merciful without condition. He told one minister to take whatever stood in his way, even from the brothers, as grace.

“No brother, however much he has sinned, should leave your presence without mercy, if he asks mercy; if he does not ask, you ask him.”

— Francis of Assisi, Letter to a Minister (our translation from the Latin)

He wrote this to a minister whose name the letter does not keep. On his deathbed he forgave all his brothers, “as well absent as present,” as Celano records.

Patience shows what we are

Francis held that a person’s worth is what he is before God, and that patience is tested only when others oppose us.

“You cannot tell how much patience and humility a servant of God has while everything pleases him. But when the people who should satisfy him do the opposite, he has as much patience and humility as he shows then, and no more.”

— Francis of Assisi, Admonition XIII (our translation from the Latin)

In another Admonition he wrote, “As much as a person is before God, so much he is, and no more.” And in another: “Where there is love and wisdom, there is neither fear nor ignorance. Where there is patience and humility, neither anger nor disturbance. Where there is poverty with joy, neither greed nor avarice.” The true peacemakers, he wrote, are those who keep peace in mind and body, whatever they suffer, for the love of Christ.

Praise through the creatures

Francis saw every creature as a brother or sister, and the whole world as a reason to praise God. He preached to birds and spoke to fire as “brother fire.”

“Praised be my Lord for our sister, mother earth, who sustains and governs us and brings forth many fruits with colored flowers and grass.”

— Francis of Assisi, Canticle of Brother Sun, San Damiano, about 1225 (our translation from the Umbrian Italian)

He made the Canticle, ill and nearly blind, in a hut near San Damiano, in the Italian of Umbria rather than Latin. Its last line sums up what he asked of everyone: “Praise and bless my Lord, give him thanks, and serve him with great humility.” Even death was “our sister, bodily death, from whom no living person can escape.”

Work and simplicity

Francis wanted his brothers to work with their hands, and he told those who could not read not to trouble about learning letters but to long for the Spirit of the Lord.

“And I worked with my own hands, and I want to work.”

— Francis of Assisi, Testament, 1226 (our translation from the Latin)

In the Testament he remembered the first days: “we were uneducated and subject to everyone.” The Rule of 1223 asks that preaching be brief and that brothers who cannot read not trouble to learn. He himself carried stones to rebuild San Damiano and begged for what he ate.

Poverty to the end

Francis wanted to follow the poverty that Christ and his mother had lived, and he asked Clare and her sisters never to leave it, whatever anyone advised them.

“I, little Brother Francis, want to follow the life and poverty of our most high Lord Jesus Christ and of his most holy mother, and to hold to it to the end.”

— Francis of Assisi, last will for Clare and her sisters (our translation from the Latin)

He wrote it shortly before he died, and Clare kept it by copying it into her own Rule. In his Testament he wrote of going back to “the Lord’s table,” begging alms from door to door. On his deathbed he would accept his habit only as a loan.

A servant to everyone

Francis called himself the servant of his brothers and of everyone. He gave up the government of the Order in 1220, saying, “Henceforth I am dead to you,” and promised obedience to the man who took his place.

“I think myself the greatest of sinners, for if God had followed any other wicked man with such great mercy he would have been tenfold more spiritual than I.”

— Francis of Assisi, in Thomas of Celano’s Second Life, 1244–47 (tr. A. G. Ferrers Howell)

He signed his letter to all Christians “brother Francis, their servant and subject,” and his Testament “your little one and servant.” When a brother urged him in his illness to have the Prophets read to him, he answered, “I need no more, my son: I know Christ, the poor man crucified.”

did_you_know.fact: Only two pieces of Francis’s own handwriting are known, Paschal Robinson wrote in 1906, and both were written for his friend Brother Leo.
The first announcement of Francis’s stigmata, Brother Elias’s letter of October 1226, mentions no mountain, no seraph, and no date.

The earliest account of Francis’s visit to the Sultan, by Bishop Jacques de Vitry, who was with the crusaders at Damietta, says nothing of a trial by fire; it says the Sultan asked Francis to pray for him.

did_you_know.fact: When his body was found in 1818 after fifty-two nights of digging, a rough stone lay under his head for a pillow.
The famous “Peace Prayer” is not his: it first appeared, unsigned, in a Paris magazine in 1912.

sources.used_for: 1978 examination (about 1.57–1.58 m); nearly 400,000 reservations in the first days; 1230, 1818 summary

gaps: Biography is 9,972 words by the lint count (narrative, source note, and research paragraph), within the tier A range.

Latin quoted in the biography is limited to lines checked against page scans (Jacques de Vitry, fol. 353). Francis’s Testament, last will for Clare, Leo letter, and Chartula, and Elias’s letter were checked against scans; Jordan of Giano, Thomas of Spalato, Jacques’s letters, and Wadding’s 1230 bull were read only in OCR and appear in our English without quotation of the Latin. The biography also prints the three-word Latin phrase Secretum meum mihi as it stands in the 1868 English Bonaventure, and the Latin titles of the bulls Solet annuere, Mira circa nos and Speravimus.
The early Lives (Celano, Three Companions, Bonaventure, Mirror, Little Flowers) were read in English translations only.

Not read: Celano’s Treatise on the Miracles, Julian of Speyer’s Life and Office, Bonaventure’s Minor Legend, the Legend of Perugia and Assisi Compilation in Latin, the rest of Jacques de Vitry’s Historia occidentalis, the Latin process of Clare, the bulls of 1237 and 1255 on the stigmata, the 1818 reports and the 1820 bull Assisiensem Basilicam, and modern studies (Tolan, Frugoni, Cooper).

Date conflicts are set out in the biography’s source note: canonization 16 July vs the bull’s dating clause; death at nightfall 3 Oct (Elias: first hour of the night before Sunday 4 Oct); stigmata day; translation 25 vs 21 May 1230 (the Catholic Encyclopedia’s article on Elias puts it a few days before 25 May; a web summary also gives 22 May); the bull Speravimus printed with an impossible date (Key to Umbria gives 16 June 1230); Clare’s flight 1212 vs about 1211.

Attributed, not stated as fact: the 1221 chapter size (Jordan about 3,000; Mirror 5,000); the 1230 seizure (Wadding and the bull, OCR); the 1818 finds (Key to Umbria); Ernoul’s two clerics (identified with Francis only by the 1871 editor, who names the Sultan “Coradin”).

Left out: the fire ordeal and the Sultan’s conversion as fact; Bona at the Portiuncula (the Process puts her in Rome); the pass-one claim that Elias saw the side wound by a trick (Celano 2C §137–138 does not say so); the Ernoul story in the narrative; the 5 October 1818 start date (search snippet only); the 1449 legend of the standing body.
Clare’s process was read only in a modern Spanish translation (facts only); no wording from it is quoted.
Orthodox commemoration not checked; venerated_in set to roman-catholic only.
The Canticle in related.prayers is partial; the Letter to the Order’s closing prayer was not translated.
Check before print: whether Pope Leo XIV’s visit to Assisi in August 2026 took place (not used in the text).
No image chosen; all candidates unverified.

name: supported
Common English name with title.
biography: All facts from the five notes files; late and legendary sources marked in the text; 17 chapters, 12 block quotes.
birth_year: Howell’s table gives 1182; the Catholic Encyclopedia gives 1181 or 1182. No source gives a day.
death_location: Portiuncula / Santa Maria degli Angeli (Celano I.105–110; Bonaventure XIV.3; Jordan §50).
feast_day_catholic: 4 October, ordered in Mira circa nos.
feast_day_orthodox: Western saint after 1054; no Orthodox commemoration checked.
categories: Ascetic, friar (Monastics is the nearest category), missionary journeys to Syria and Morocco, miracles in the early Lives, patron of Italy and ecology.
patron: Italy 1939 (Wikipedia, facts-only); ecology 1979 (Inter Sanctos via EWTN). Popular patronages not researched.
relic_description: Catholic Encyclopedia, Jordan of Giano, Wadding, Key to Umbria and OFM Conv. news pages (facts only), Robinson, Celano.
relic_location: Lower Basilica crypt, built under Pius VII (Wikipedia; Catholic Encyclopedia).
miracles: 79 entries: the list Celano says was read at the canonization (21), life (24), Second Life and Mirror (23), death (4), after death (7), each with status and source. No entry is labelled approved by the Church, because the bull names no miracle.
teachings: Nine themes from his writings and sayings, our translations and Howell’s Celano.
quotes: 49 quotes; his writings in our translation (scan-checked where marked), sayings from Howell’s 1908 Celano, one line from Jacques de Vitry.
prayers: Partial texts kept in the packet only; Peace Prayer excluded.
